questions.text: What is the firm's objective in the cost-minimization problem at a given output?

options.a: Select the lowest feasible output price.
options.b: Maximize market demand.
options.c: Choose a feasible input combination that minimizes total input expenditure.
options.d: Maximize output regardless of input expenditure.

questions.text: What does the cost function c(w1,w2,y) measure?

options.a: Maximum revenue at those input prices.
options.b: Average utility of consuming y units.
options.c: Minimum cost of producing y units at input prices w1 and w2.
options.d: The minimum income necessary to buy both inputs as final consumption.

questions.text: What does an isocost line represent?

options.a: Output quantities with identical marginal cost.
options.b: Consumer bundles with the same satisfaction.
options.c: Input bundles with the same physical output.
options.d: Input bundles with the same total expenditure.

questions.text: What is the slope of an isocost line with input 2 on the vertical axis and input 1 on the horizontal axis?

options.d: -MP1/MP2 regardless of input choice.

questions.text: Why is the cost-minimizing input choice a point on the lowest attainable isocost line?

options.a: Isocost lines correspond to different utility levels.
options.b: The firm seeks to maximize fixed costs.
options.c: Higher isocost lines always yield lower output.
options.d: All higher isocost lines imply greater expenditure for the required output.

questions.text: For smooth isoquants and an interior optimum, what tangency condition must hold?

options.a: Input quantities must be identical.
options.b: MP1/MP2 = w1/w2.
options.c: MP1+MP2 = w1+w2.
options.d: MP1/w1 = w2/MP2.

questions.text: What is the economic meaning of MP1/w1 = MP2/w2 at an interior cost minimum?

options.a: Both inputs must have the same price.
options.b: Each euro spent on either input yields the same marginal output.
options.c: Marginal costs must be zero.
options.d: Total output is equal for both inputs.

questions.text: If the marginal output per euro spent on labor exceeds that of capital at an interior input choice, how can cost be lowered at fixed output?

options.a: Decrease output permanently.
options.b: Use relatively more capital and less labor.
options.c: Increase both inputs in equal quantities.
options.d: Use relatively more labor and less capital until the marginal product per euro is equalized.

questions.text: Which constraint must a conditional factor demand satisfy?

options.a: Produce at least the specified output level at least cost.
options.b: Keep consumer utility fixed.
options.c: Maximize profit for a fixed market demand.
options.d: Maximize output price.

questions.text: Conditional factor demand functions depend on which variables?

options.a: Input prices and required output.
options.b: Monopoly demand elasticity alone.
options.c: Income and consumer tastes only.
options.d: The firm's fixed market share only.

questions.text: For f(x1,x2)=min(x1,x2) and positive factor prices, which input combination minimizes cost for output y?

options.a: x1=y and x2=0.
options.b: x1=2y and x2=0.
options.c: x1=0 and x2=y.
options.d: x1=y and x2=y.

questions.text: Under f(x1,x2)=min(x1,x2), what is the long-run cost function?

options.d: min(w1,w2)y.

questions.text: For f(x1,x2)=x1+x2 with strictly unequal positive input prices, what is cost-minimizing production?

options.a: Use only the cheaper input.
options.b: Use only the more expensive input.
options.c: Use no inputs and still produce y.
options.d: Use the two inputs in equal quantities.

questions.text: For f(x1,x2)=x1+x2, what is the long-run cost function?

options.a: min(w1,w2)y.
options.c: max(w1,w2)y.

questions.text: Why might an input cost minimum occur at a corner instead of a smooth tangency?

options.a: Inputs may be perfect substitutes or an interior tangency may not be optimal or feasible.
options.b: Input prices must be zero.
options.c: A corner cannot be cost minimizing under any technology.
options.d: Isoquants must always be tangent at every corner.

questions.text: When one input becomes more expensive relative to another at fixed output under a smooth convex technology, what substitution is usually expected?

options.a: Away from the more expensive input toward the cheaper input.
options.b: Toward the more expensive input.
options.c: Away from every input simultaneously while keeping output fixed.
options.d: Toward both inputs in identical proportions irrespective of technology.

questions.text: If the wage rises holding the rental rate of capital fixed, how does the isocost slope -w/r change with labor horizontally measured?

options.a: It becomes positive.
options.b: It becomes flatter.
options.c: It becomes steeper in absolute value.
options.d: It stays unchanged.

questions.text: What is an expansion path?

options.a: The path followed by prices as consumer income rises.
options.b: A line joining equal-profit bundles.
options.c: A producer-surplus curve as output is taxed.
options.d: The locus of cost-minimizing input bundles as output varies at fixed input prices.

questions.text: What is a normal input in conditional factor demand?

options.a: An input whose cost-minimizing use falls when output rises.
options.b: An input whose cost-minimizing use rises when required output rises.
options.c: An input whose price falls when output rises.
options.d: An input whose marginal product is always increasing.

questions.text: What is an inferior input in conditional factor demand?

options.a: An input that can never be productive.
options.b: An input with a negative market price.
options.c: An input whose use necessarily falls when its own price falls.
options.d: An input whose cost-minimizing use falls as required output rises, at fixed input prices.

questions.text: Why can the expansion path bend toward one input as the firm scales up?

options.a: Input prices must change with output.
options.b: Total cost always falls as output rises.
options.c: The least-cost input mix can change with output because technology need not be homothetic.
options.d: Every cost-minimizing bundle has identical input ratios.

questions.text: How is the cost function obtained from conditional input demands?

options.a: Differentiate total revenue with respect to price.
options.b: Insert the cost-minimizing input quantities into the expenditure expression.
options.c: Insert Marshallian demand into the consumer's utility function.
options.d: Add the factor prices without accounting for quantities.

questions.text: What does Shephard's lemma in production theory say?

options.a: The partial derivative of profit with respect to output price equals conditional labor demand.
options.b: The partial derivative of minimum cost with respect to an input price equals conditional demand for that input.
options.c: The second derivative of cost with respect to output is always zero.
options.d: The derivative of output with respect to input prices equals revenue.

questions.text: If c(w1,w2,y) is differentiable, what does dc/dw1 equal?

options.a: The output price.
options.b: The marginal cost of output.
options.c: The negative of optimal output.
options.d: The cost-minimizing quantity of input 1.

questions.text: Why is a cost function nondecreasing in input prices?

options.a: A rise in an input price cannot make producing the same output cheaper at any unchanged feasible input combination.
options.b: Average fixed cost always rises at the same rate.
options.c: Higher input prices make technologies more efficient.
options.d: Firms always increase output when prices rise.

questions.text: What is the homogeneity of the cost function in all input prices?

options.a: It is homogeneous of degree one in input prices.
options.b: It is homogeneous of degree zero in input prices.
options.c: It is homogeneous of degree two in input prices.
options.d: It is independent of all input prices.

questions.text: If both input prices double and technology and output stay fixed, what happens to minimum cost?

options.a: It halves.
options.b: It is unchanged.
options.c: It quadruples.
options.d: It doubles.

questions.text: Under standard technology, how is minimum cost shaped as a function of input prices?

options.a: It is necessarily convex in input prices.
options.b: It is independent of relative input prices.
options.c: It is concave in input prices.
options.d: It is always strictly linear in each individual price.

questions.text: What does the marginal cost of output equal when the cost function is differentiable in output?

options.a: The partial derivative of c(w,y) with respect to y.
options.b: The sum of conditional factor quantities.
options.c: The derivative of consumer expenditure with respect to price.
options.d: The wage divided by the rental rate.

questions.text: With constant returns to scale and constant input prices, how does minimum total cost change when output doubles?

options.a: It becomes independent of output.
options.b: It more than doubles.
options.c: It doubles.
options.d: It less than doubles.

questions.text: With increasing returns to scale, what cost behavior is associated with expanding output proportionally at fixed input prices?

options.a: Input prices must fall to zero.
options.b: Long-run cost rises less than proportionally, under the usual cost-minimization assumptions.
options.c: Long-run cost rises more than proportionally.
options.d: Long-run cost always equals zero.

questions.text: With decreasing returns to scale, what happens to the long-run average cost as scale expands, in the standard model?

options.a: It stays exactly constant.
options.b: It becomes negative.
options.c: It tends to increase.
options.d: It must decrease.

questions.text: What is the connection between increasing returns to scale and economies of scale?

options.a: Increasing returns always generate rising long-run average cost.
options.b: They are unrelated to cost behavior.
options.c: Increasing returns generally generate declining long-run average cost at fixed input prices.
options.d: Economies of scale mean marginal products are all negative.

questions.text: How does the short-run cost-minimization problem differ from the long-run problem?

options.a: All inputs are freely adjustable in the short run but not in the long run.
options.b: At least one input is constrained at a fixed level in the short run.
options.c: Short-run firms never face input prices.
options.d: Long-run firms must produce only zero output.

questions.text: At any required output, how do optimized long-run costs compare with costs under an arbitrary fixed short-run input level?

options.a: Short-run costs are always zero.
options.b: Long-run costs must be strictly higher.
options.c: Long-run costs are independent of technology.
options.d: Long-run costs cannot be higher because the firm has more input choices.

questions.text: When do short-run and long-run total costs coincide at a particular output?

options.a: When the short-run fixed factor equals the long-run optimal factor choice for that output.
options.b: At every output irrespective of plant size.
options.c: Only when output is zero.
options.d: Whenever labor and capital have the same price.

questions.text: Why is it incorrect to regard any arbitrarily chosen plant size as long-run cost minimizing?

options.a: Long-run optimization holds all input levels fixed.
options.b: Plant size never affects costs.
options.c: Long-run optimization chooses plant size jointly with other inputs.
options.d: Output price directly determines the cheapest input bundle without technology.

questions.text: What changes when an input price rises, with output required to stay fixed?

options.a: Minimum cost necessarily falls.
options.b: Minimum cost weakly rises, and the firm may substitute away from that input.
options.c: Minimum cost always stays unchanged.
options.d: The production function shifts outward automatically.

questions.text: What is the distinction between a cost function and a production function?

options.a: Both map prices to consumer utility.
options.b: The production function gives maximal output from inputs; the cost function gives minimum expenditure for output at factor prices.
options.c: A cost function is independent of input prices.
options.d: A production function is necessarily expressed in euros.

questions.text: What does the envelope theorem imply about the marginal cost of output at an optimized factor mix?

options.a: It must be negative under all increasing returns.
options.b: It equals average fixed cost at every output.
options.c: It does not depend on the production process.
options.d: It captures the marginal resource cost of producing an additional unit with inputs optimally adjusted.

questions.text: At the smooth cost-minimizing tangency in the diagram, what must equal the relative input price?

options.a: The absolute technical rate of substitution MP1/MP2.
options.b: The ratio of input quantities x1/x2 in every technology.
options.c: The average cost of producing the final good.
options.d: Total output divided by total cost.
